Cleaning 209 frames (99 mediums and 110 deeps) by hand is a massive, tedious undertaking, especially when dealing with the level of buildup shown in file "8d6e9411-4818-4929-9330-c1fc385e3d11".

Your instincts to use heat and change the workflow are exactly on target. Cold-scraping propolis and old wax is incredibly inefficient. Here is how to overhaul this process into a highly efficient assembly line.

Evaluating Your Ideas

  • Heating the hive tool: While clever in theory, a standard metal hive tool loses its heat almost instantly when it touches cold wax and wood. You would spend more time reheating the tool than scraping.
  • Soaking in water: Simply soaking them in cold or warm water will ruin the wood (causing warping and rot) without touching the wax, which repels water.
  • Heating/Incubating: This is the golden ticket. Wax melts around 145°F (63°C). If you heat the frame, the wax and propolis turn to butter, and the debris wipes right off.

The Ultimate Assembly Line: The Boiling Dip Method

Given the volume of frames, the presence of mouse droppings, and the need to clear out moth webs, the most efficient commercial-style approach is a boiling water dip. This allows you to process frames in batches, melting the wax and sterilizing the wood simultaneously.

Setting this up in an open staging ground or a workshop garage yard is ideal, as it is a messy process.

The Setup:

  1. The Vat: You need a large metal vessel—a galvanized trash can, a 55-gallon steel drum cut in half, or a very large turkey fryer pot.
  2. The Heat: A propane turkey fryer burner positioned underneath the vessel to bring the water to a rolling boil.
  3. The Solution: Add a small amount of dish soap or washing soda to the boiling water. This helps separate the wax and breaks down the sticky propolis.

The Workflow:

  1. Triage (Do this first): Don't lay everything out on the ground. Use empty supers as your sorting bins. Go through your 22 boxes and quickly sort the frames straight into "Keep/Clean," "Replace Foundation," and "Trash" (for the mouse-chewed ones).
  2. The Boil: Using heavy-duty rubber gloves and tongs, dunk 3 to 5 frames into the boiling water for about 2–3 minutes.
  3. The Shake: Pull them out. The boiling water will have melted the wax and sterilized the mouse droppings. Most of the gunk will simply fall off or float to the top of the vat (which you can skim off later).
  4. The Quick Scrape: While the wood is still piping hot, take your hive tool and quickly glide it over the frame. The remaining propolis and wax will slide off with zero resistance.
  5. Dry: Stack them crisscrossed in the sun so the hot wood dries rapidly without warping.

Alternative: The Heat Gun Station

If a boiling vat isn't feasible, a heat gun is your next best option for an assembly line.

  1. Clamp a heat gun to a workbench, pointing outward, leaving both of your hands free.
  2. Put on thick leather or insulated rubber gloves.
  3. Hold the frame in the stream of the heat gun. As the wax begins to bubble and melt, drag your hive tool across it.
  4. This isolates the heat exactly where you are scraping, eliminating the mechanical friction of cold-scraping.

Solving the "Inside Rail" Problem

Scraping the inside groove where the foundation sits is notoriously the worst part of the job. A standard hive tool isn't shaped for it.

Instead of struggling with a makeshift scraper, you can quickly design and print a custom channel-scraper on a Bambu Lab A1.

  • Take exact caliper measurements of the top and bottom frame grooves.
  • Print a small, rigid handheld jig (using PETG or ABS for heat/impact resistance) with a protruding lip that perfectly matches the groove's profile.
  • After heating the frame, you can drag this custom tool through the channel once, plowing all the melted wax and debris out in a single, satisfying swipe.

Radiant Heat vs. Convection Loss

  • The Heat Engine (Winning): The direct radiant heat from the UV 9 sunlight hitting your flat black interior will superheat the wood and the air immediately touching it. The frames themselves will absorb this radiant heat very quickly.
  • The Leak (Losing): Because hot air rises, an unsealed glass pane or gaps between the boxes will act like a chimney. The superheated air will draft out of the top, and cooler 87°F air will pull in through the gaps at the bottom.

The Expected Results

Instead of acting like a pressurized pressure cooker, your box will act more like an open-faced grill with a lid resting on it.

  • Peak Temperature: Instead of soaring to 180°F+ (which a sealed box would do under UV 9), the internal temperature will likely plateau between 150°F and 155°F. This is just above the 145°F melting point of beeswax, so it will still work.
  • Time Penalty: In a sealed box at 87°F/UV 9, the wax would melt in about 60 minutes. Because you are constantly losing hot air through the unsealed gaps, expect it to take 90 to 110 minutes to fully melt a batch of 10 frames.
  • The Propolis Factor: Propolis has a slightly higher melting point than beeswax. In a "leaky" box, the wax will melt off, but the propolis might just turn into a thick, sticky gum rather than turning fully liquid.

The Lean Solution

If you want to avoid dealing with foam weatherstripping or taping the seams, you can achieve a "good enough" seal just by using gravity.

Standard bee boxes are machined to sit flush. If you just lay the glass on top and place a couple of heavy bricks or rocks on the corners of the glass, the weight will compress the wooden seams of the deep box and the 3-inch spacer together.
